StatisticalMechanics/en/181.response:
The spectral radiance per unit wavelength of a blackbody is  

\[
B_\lambda(\lambda ,T)=\frac{2hc^{2}}{\lambda^{5}}\,
\frac{1}{\exp\!\Big(\frac{hc}{\lambda kT}\Big)-1}\, .
\]

The maximum occurs where \(\partial B_\lambda/\partial\lambda=0\).  Using  

\[
x\equiv\frac{hc}{\lambda kT},
\qquad\lambda=\frac{hc}{xkT},
\]

the condition \(\partial B_\lambda/\partial\lambda=0\) reduces to  

\[
\frac{x e^{x}}{e^{x}-1}=5
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=5\bigl(1-e^{-x}\bigr) .
\]

The transcendental equation has the unique positive root  

\[
x_{\rm peak}\approx 4.96511423 .
\]

Substituting \(x_{\rm peak}\) back into \(\lambda = hc/(xkT)\) gives  

\[
\lambda_{\max}=\frac{hc}{k\,x_{\rm peak}}\;\frac{1}{T}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\lambda_{\max}T=\frac{hc}{k\,x_{\rm peak}} .
\]

Evaluating the constants  

\[
\frac{hc}{k}=1.4387770\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m\,K},
\qquad 
\frac{hc}{k\,x_{\rm peak}}
   \approx\frac{1.4387770\times10^{-2}}{4.96511423}
   =2.8977719\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m\,K}.
\]

Thus Wien’s displacement law follows:

\[
\boxed{\lambda_{\max}\,T = b \approx 2.898\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m\,K},
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\lambda_{\max}= \frac{b}{T}\,.}
\]

Starting from Planck’s spectral radiance (energy emitted per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit wavelength interval)

\[
b_{\lambda}= \frac{2\,h\,c^{2}}{\lambda^{5}}\,
          \frac{1}{\displaystyle e^{\frac{h c}{\lambda k T}}-1},
\]

the energy of a single photon of wavelength $\lambda$ is  

\[
E_{\text{ph}}=\frac{h c}{\lambda}.
\]

The photon flux (number of photons per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit wavelength interval) is obtained by dividing the radiance by the photon energy:

\[
n_{\lambda}
   =\frac{b_{\lambda}}{E_{\text{ph}}}
   =\frac{2\,h\,c^{2}}{\lambda^{5}}
     \frac{1}{e^{\frac{h c}{\lambda k T}}-1}\;
     \frac{\lambda}{h c}
   =\frac{2c}{\lambda^{4}}\,
     \frac{1}{e^{\frac{h c}{\lambda k T}}-1}.
\]

If the wavelength interval is expressed in microns, one multiplies by
$1\;\mu\text{m}=10^{-6}\,$ m; the functional form of $n_{\lambda}$ is unchanged.

\[
\boxed{\,n_{\lambda}= \frac{2c}{\lambda^{4}\!\left(e^{\,h c/(\lambda k T)}-1\right)}\,}
\]

QuantumMechanics/en/357.response:
For a weak magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}=B\hat z\) the Zeeman perturbation is  

\[
H'=\mu_{B}B\frac{L_{z}+g_{S}S_{z}}{\hbar},\qquad g_{S}\simeq2 .
\]

Using first–order perturbation theory the energy shift of an unperturbed LS–coupled state
\(|\,l\,s\,j\,m_{j}\rangle\) is  

\[
\Delta E^{(1)}_{jm_{j}}
 =\left\langle l s j m_{j}\right|H'\left|l s j m_{j}\right\rangle
 =\mu_{B}B\,\frac{\langle L_{z}\rangle+g_{S}\langle S_{z}\rangle}{\hbar}.
\]

In the LS–coupled basis  

\[
\langle L_{z}\rangle
 =\frac{j(j+1)+l(l+1)-s(s+1)}{2j(j+1)}\,m_{j}\hbar,
\qquad
\langle S_{z}\rangle
 =\frac{j(j+1)-l(l+1)+s(s+1)}{2j(j+1)}\,m_{j}\hbar,
\]

so that  

\[
\langle L_{z}+g_{S}S_{z}\rangle
 =g_{j}\,m_{j}\hbar,
\qquad
g_{j}=1+\frac{j(j+1)+s(s+1)-l(l+1)}{2j(j+1)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\Delta E^{(1)}_{jm_{j}}=\mu_{B}B\,g_{j}m_{j}
\equiv\varepsilon\,g_{j}m_{j},
\qquad \varepsilon\equiv\mu_{B}B\ll W .
\]

For the case \(l=1\) (p–electron) and \(s=\tfrac12\) the possible total‑angular‑momentum values are
\(j=\tfrac12,\tfrac32\).  
For \(j=\tfrac32\),

\[
g_{3/2}=1+\frac{\tfrac34+\tfrac34-2}{2\cdot\tfrac34}
      =1+\frac{1/2}{3/2}= \frac{4}{3}.
\]

Thus the Zeeman shifts are  

\[
\Delta E^{(1)}_{3/2,m_{j}}
 =\varepsilon\,\frac{4}{3}\,m_{j},
\qquad m_{j}= \frac32,\;\frac12,\;-\frac12,\;-\frac32 .
\]

Evaluating for each \(m_{j}\) gives

\[
\boxed{\Delta E_{j=3/2,m_j}
 =\varepsilon\frac{4}{3}m_j
 =\begin{cases}
   +2\varepsilon & (m_j=+\tfrac32),\\[4pt]
   +\tfrac{2}{3}\varepsilon & (m_j=+\tfrac12),\\[4pt]
   -\tfrac{2}{3}\varepsilon & (m_j=-\tfrac12),\\[4pt]
   -2\varepsilon & (m_j=-\tfrac32)\;. 
   \end{cases}} \]

Equivalently, the probability that a photon is observed between polar angles \(\theta\) and \(\theta+d\theta\) (integrating over the azimuthal angle) is

QuantumMechanics/en/650.response:
Using the Pauli‑matrix algebra  

\[
[\sigma_i,\sigma_j]=2\,\mathrm i\,\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k,\qquad 
\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}=2\delta_{ij}{\mathbb I},\qquad 
\sigma_i^{2}={\mathbb I},
\]

and the definitions \(\sigma_{\pm}\equiv\sigma_x\pm\mathrm i\sigma_y\) we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
[\sigma_{+},\sigma_{-}]
&=[\sigma_x+\mathrm i\sigma_y,\;\sigma_x-\mathrm i\sigma_y]  \\
&=-\,\mathrm i[\sigma_x,\sigma_y]+\mathrm i[\sigma_y,\sigma_x]   \\
&= -\,\mathrm i(2\mathrm i\sigma_z)+\mathrm i(-2\mathrm i\sigma_z)
=4\sigma_z ,\\[4pt]
[\sigma_z,\sigma_{\pm}]
&=[\sigma_z,\sigma_x]\pm\mathrm i[\sigma_z,\sigma_y]  \\
&=2\mathrm i\sigma_y\pm\mathrm i(-2\mathrm i\sigma_x)
= \pm2(\sigma_x\pm\mathrm i\sigma_y)
=\pm2\sigma_{\pm}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the squares,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\sigma_{+})^{2}
&=(\sigma_x+\mathrm i\sigma_y)^2
    =\sigma_x^{2}+ \mathrm i\{\sigma_x,\sigma_y\}-\sigma_y^{2} \\
&={\mathbb I}+ \mathrm i\!\cdot\!0-{\mathbb I}=0,\\[4pt]
(\sigma_{-})^{2}
&=(\sigma_x-\mathrm i\sigma_y)^2
    =\sigma_x^{2}- \mathrm i\{\sigma_x,\sigma_y\}-\sigma_y^{2}
    ={\mathbb I}-\mathrm i\!\cdot\!0-{\mathbb I}=0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\;[\sigma_{+},\sigma_{-}]=4\sigma_{z},\qquad
[\sigma_{z},\sigma_{\pm}]=\pm2\sigma_{\pm},\qquad
(\sigma_{\pm})^{2}=0\;
}
\]

Here \(V\) is the potential difference between the inner and outer conductors, \(Q\) the total free charge on the inner sphere, and the effective permittivity that enters the field is the angular average

QuantumMechanics/en/229.response:
\[

\frac{d\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}}{dt}
   =\frac{i}{\hbar}\Big[\,H,\;\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\,\Big]
   =\frac{i}{\hbar}\Big[-\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{B}(\mathbf r ,t),
                       \;\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\Big]
   =\frac{g\,e}{2m}\;\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\times\mathbf{B}(\mathbf r ,t)
\;}
\]

Equivalently, in components  

\[

\frac{d\mu_{s,i}}{dt}= \frac{g\,e}{2m}\,\epsilon_{ijk}\,
